item.title: Re: A Pain in the Back
item.content:encoded:
+ Open for critique
- Behold!

A dark take on getting a bad back from an old mattress. After a grisly murder where a child's spine was torn out of her body (and is missing), crime scene investigators noted the lack of blood on her twin size mattress, although the sheets were saturated. The SCP Foundation secures the mattress as SCP-XXXX. But what if the mattress itself isn't the problem?

Not a bad start. I'm just confused as to why the Foundation would deem the mattress as an SCP or why they're even involved at all. I feel like you should start this off as some sort of a law enforcement investigation. The oddities found during that prompt the Foundation to look into this and eventually get involved.

Journal entries describe the following story: a mom gets a mattress from a freecycling site when her older daughter is ready for a "big girl bed." The child first complains that her mattress is bumpy, then that it moves at night, and finally runs into her room after dreaming about a skeletal creature in her mattress that "wants my back, because its back hurts."

While I do really like this, I feel like journal entries wouldn't convey this successfully. I feel that this should be don't by a comprehensive description of the mattress during an investigation and interviews with the mother.

When the mattress is cut open, there is no sign of what is causing the lumps.

A bit cliche, but nothing world-ending.

When it was discovered that the SCP could move, researchers investigated locations near the mattress for potential causes of the anomaly. They discovered that an elderly man with lordosis (swayback) passed away near the murdered child. He was known to say he'd sell his soul to have a young person's spine again. Relationship not yet established

I'm not sure how I feel about this section. There are pros and cons to having it. The monster being able to switch mattresses is scary, but you already have this story about a child dying and this other section could potentially overshadow that. Focus on one element, I would recommend the story of the child and mother and do it well instead of spreading yourself thin.

They discovered that an elderly man with lordosis (swayback) passed away near the murdered child. He was known to say he'd sell his soul to have a young person's spine again. Relationship not yet established

This feels a bit cartoonish juxtaposed against what you previously have. Also, not everything needs to be explained. Horror comes from not showing the monster. That being said, you can have the monster send some form of a parting message using the bumps. I imagine them realizing that the bumps spell out the word "MORE" or something like that.

Overall, this has legs. I'd like for you to clean up the idea and streamline your narrative. This will help with really concentrating those horror elements while not taking away from the narrative you're proposing. I'll give a tentative greenlight as long as you take into account some of my recommendations. Good luck!

item.title: Re: A Pain in the Back
item.content:encoded:
So, although I recognize that you’ve put a lot of effort and energy into this concept… it feels like a well laid out “murder monster”

In terms of adding narrative, consider the following questions and in answering them, edit your original idea to reflect:

  • what is the overall arc of this story? Merely the discovery of the monster, or is there more to it?
  • Often times a shallow seeming horror story can be a vehicle for discussion of larger thematic elements… what do you want your story to communicate to the reader? What’s the take away?
  • Consider adding some depth to this creature… why does it do this?
  • From who’s perspective is the story going to be? And why should the reader care? (How will you engage the reader to be invested in these events?)

item.title: Re: A Pain in the Back
item.content:encoded:
I'm in agony right now, so please take the reviw that follows with a small MINE of salt, but…

+ show block
– hide block

Place holder, will finish this review at the ER…

The agony that sent me to the hospital was so severe that I was able to get nothing done while I was there, but now I am at home again, with a mild analgesic to numb the area in question so let me try once more.

Initial Impressions: And this is why this green-lighting process is stupid and counter-productive: this is already ready to be written up as an article and were it within my power you would have your first Green-Light.

Elevator Pitch: This concept is unique and AFAIK, we have nothing like it: I find it solid and compelling it grabs you and doesn't let-go.

Central Narrative: This story is original and informative, I would like to see where it goes. Of especially great merit is that the primary researcher looses lock and this is when things go wrong.

Hook: Crossed out containment procedures is a nice touch, but might be slightly over-used: I advise caution.

Additional Notes: The personal connection might be extraneous, but it was interesting to read.

In Summary: This should already have been green-lighted; I find it baffling that it's not.

Let me re-iterate: I am half-mad with pain as I write this; you should not take this as gospel.

item.title: Re: A Pain in the Back
item.content:encoded:
Let's see what we have here.

[+] Here, have some crit
[-] OK, now give me back my crit

First of all, you should specify that the "true" anomaly is a monster that can hide itself inside the mattress, as you told me in #thecritters. Just so reviewers don't become confusion.

After several tests […]

Why didn't they check inside the mattress during this time? I think it would be some of the very first things they do. You may give the monster some "hidding abilities" to cover this up.

[…] primary researcher goes on sabbatical and the tests are paused […]

This is weird for me. I don't think the Foundation would stop the tests if this is a newly discovered anomaly. If the researcher goes on vacations, they would assign someone else. Maybe the staff member complaint about the floor in between tests?

I plan to have the diary entries of the child's mom (explaining the monster her child describes leading up to the murder) […]

I think you should focus on this. The diary of a mother becoming more concerned about her child seeing monsters can be pretty terrifying, not to mention that you already "know" what's it like "to have a monster inside your mattress". But the thing that bugges me is that you'll have to describe the monster and its abilities in the Description, so it will not be as surprising as it needs to. Maybe you can write the "old" document and then add an addendum saying the new discoveries and that the document is pending updates?

a D-class who was moved to this room after repeatedly complaining about every roommate they were assigned.

Nope. The Foundation is a prison, not an student dormitory. If the D-Class don't like their "roommate", that's up to them. The Foundation would only separate them if they're a risk to each other. Maybe you can still write the experiment log without this part?

Overall, this has some plot holes and inconsistencies, but I think it can work as a Horror article.

Feel free to contact a member of the Butterfly Squad to get more crit, or PM me to take another look.

I got summed back.

[+] Here, have some more crit
[-] OK, now give me back my crit

So my concern is that this might fall under the category of "just another spooky monster". I was wondering that maybe it would be better to never show the monster. At all. Maybe the Foundation knows that there is a monster, but they never get to see it? Maybe they just discover the bodies and eventually the figure out that there is a creature hidding in the mattres?

Also, just finding the bodies of the researchers would feel a little sour. Maybe you can write the transcription of video logs from the surveillance cameras? That way you could add some more spooky atmosphere.

Furthermore, I think you may want to read this essay about horror in the SCP format.

Overall, this can be very spooky, but be careful to not fall under "just another monster".

Feel free to contact a member of the Butterfly Squad to get more crit, or PM me to take another look

(I highly recommed reaching out to other people, since I can't hand out greenlights yet.)

item.title: A Pain in the Back
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre: Horror

Page Layout: Special Containment Procedures, Description, Discovery Notes, Journal Entries, Test Notes, Incident Report

Elevator Pitch: A dark take on getting a bad back from an old mattress. After a grisly murder where a child's spine was torn out of her body (and is missing), crime scene investigators noted the lack of blood on her twin size mattress, although the sheets were saturated. The SCP Foundation secures the mattress as SCP-XXXX. But what if the mattress itself isn't the problem?

Central Narrative: Journal entries describe the following story: a mom gets a mattress from a freecycling site when her older daughter is ready for a "big girl bed." The child first complains that her mattress is bumpy, then that it moves at night, and finally runs into her room after dreaming about a skeletal creature in her mattress that "wants my back, because its back hurts." The mom lets the girl sleep with her that night, but insists that the little girl sleeps in her own bed the following night. The next night the child is killed and the journal is confiscated along with the mattress. Research reveals nothing unusual in mattress's history, and no clear explanation for how it became anomalous.

After recovery of SCP-XXXX, months of tests show that any vertebrate (living or dead, human or non-human) suffers the same fate. There are 26 distinct lumps in the mattress, (the same as the number of bones in a human spine). The length of these lumps corresponds to the size of the previous victim, but the "spine" is seriously deformed. When the mattress is cut open, there is no sign of what is causing the lumps.

After the primary researcher is injured in a containment breach (of another SCP), testing is paused for several weeks. During this time, one researcher complains to maintenance about bumps in the hallway outside of SCPs room. The following day, this researcher is found deceased, with their spine ripped away, lying on an old couch in their office. Apparently, SCP-XXXX is a creature that moved from the mattress to the couch through the floor when ignored.

When it was discovered that the SCP could move, researchers investigated locations near the mattress for potential causes of the anomaly. They discovered that an elderly man with lordosis (swayback) passed away near the murdered child. He was known to say he'd sell his soul to have a young person's spine again. Relationship not yet established
